https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Shell rewards investors after profits soar to $9.6bn
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
First-quarter profits at Shell have risen to a record $9.6 billion as a strong performance from its secretive energy trading business helped to outweigh a fall in oil and gas prices.
The oil major revealed the profit jump and then immediately rewarded investors by announcing it would buy back $4 billion of its own shares over the next three months, after a $4 billion buyback over the previous quarter. The buybacks come on top of a $2 billion quarterly dividend.
However, the results triggered fresh calls for tougher windfall taxes amid the continuing cost of living crisis.
Analysts had expected Shell’s first-quarter adjusted earnings to fall to just under $8 billion, compared with the $9.1 billion it reported in the same three-month period of 2022, its previous record for the first quarter. Instead, profits rose, driven by higher liquefied natural gas production and Shell’s chemicals and fuels division, as well as the strong performance by its energy traders.
Wael Sawan, the chief executive, said Shell had “delivered strong results and robust operational performance, against a backdrop of volatility, while continuing to provide vital supplies of secure energy”.
Shell, which operates in more than 70 countries, reported record profits of $39.9 billion last year as oil and gas prices soared because of supply fears after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Prices eased in the latter part of 2022 amid concerns about a global economic slowdown, which would hit demand.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark price, averaged $81 a barrel in the first quarter of 2023, down from $102 in the same period a year earlier. This resulted in lower profits for Shell’s oil and gas production division.
Shell does not disclose how much its traders make, but this week analysts at Bernstein estimated that the oil company’s trading division had accounted for a fifth of profits last year.
The government has imposed a windfall tax on North Sea producers that raises the effective rate to 75 per cent. Shell has said it incurred a $134 million tax bill under the windfall levy last year and it expects to pay in excess of $500 million in windfall tax this year. It declined to disclose how much it had paid in the first quarter, saying its payment would be heavily weighted toward the end of the year.
Sharon Graham, general secretary of Unite, the union, said: “The scale of profiteering displayed today by Shell and earlier this week by BP is one of the corporate scandals of our times. And this is practically untouched by Rishi Sunak’s so-called windfall tax.”
Labour has vowed it will impose a tougher windfall tax, closing what it describes as “loopholes”, such as investment tax relief that enables companies to cut their windfall tax bill if they spend on developing new oil and gasfields.
Shell is seeking to offload its British household energy supply business as it conducts a review of the division. Sawan, 48, said he hoped to provide an update on the future of the business “in coming weeks”. The sale is thought to have attracted interest from suppliers including British Gas, Octopus and Ovo.
Reports in Russian media in recent weeks have suggested that Shell is in line for a $1.2 billion payment from Novatek after President Putin authorised it to acquire the stake in a liquefied natural gas project that Russia expropriated from Shell after it announced its intention to exit the project last year. Sinead Gorman, Shell’s chief financial officer, said “no payment has been made” and the company was reserving its legal rights in relation to the stake.
Sawan also reiterated that he believed Shell was significantly undervalued compared with its American peers, but said that relocating was not on his “priority list”.
Shell’s shares rose 20p, or 0.9 per cent, to close at £23.45½.
